--- title: "Uneven sampling and extrapolation" description: "A model answers for conditions its survey never reached, with nothing to show that it is guessing. A range check on each input misses cold, shallow winter water that a summer survey never met; the distance to the nearest surveyed station finds it, and a random forest's error grows with that distance." order: 4 categories: [assumptions] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Survey effort leaves conditions a model has never seen Survey effort is never spread evenly over the sea. It follows ports, weather, ship time and the questions of the day, so some conditions are sampled hundreds of times and others never. **Uneven sampling** means some conditions are covered thinly, so a model's fit there rests on a few stations. **Extrapolation** means predicting for conditions the survey did not cover at all. A model still answers there, and nothing in the answer shows that it is guessing. Each method carries on past the data in its own way: linear regression keeps its slope, while decision trees, random forests and k-nearest neighbours level off at the edge of the data. [Choosing a method](../03-supervised-learning/choosing-a-method.qmd#beyond-the-sampled-temperatures-each-model-follows-its-own-rule) draws three of them side by side. None of them says when it has left the data, so this page measures how far a station lies from the survey. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The distance to the nearest surveyed station shows where a model is guessing The usual check takes each input in turn and asks whether a station's value lies between the smallest and largest the survey recorded. It misses a station that is inside every range but in a combination of conditions the survey never met, such as shallow water as cold as the survey found only at depth. A check that looks at all the inputs together measures the **distance to the nearest surveyed station**: the distance [k-nearest neighbours](../03-supervised-learning/nearest-neighbours.qmd) uses to find its neighbours, with the inputs standardised so that each counts alike. A station far from every surveyed station is one the model knows little about, whatever each input says alone. Conditions the survey covered thinly lie further from their nearest station too, so the same distance shows uneven sampling. ::: {.diagram} ![A range check takes each input alone, so a shallow, cold station passes because its depth and its temperature each lie inside the survey's range. The distance to the nearest surveyed station takes all the inputs together and flags it, because the survey never met shallow, cold water.](img/range-and-distance.svg){fig-alt="Two cards, each a chart of depth across and temperature down on which the surveyed stations form a band from warm, shallow water to cold, deep water. Range check, each input alone: a dashed box spans the survey's range of depth and of temperature, and a new shallow, cold station sits inside it, so it passes. Distance to the survey, all inputs together: a line joins the same station to its nearest surveyed station across empty space, so it is flagged as far; a second new station inside the band has a short line and is close. A note says the inputs are standardised first, as for k-nearest neighbours."} ::: ## Worked example Suppose a survey sailed only in summer and autumn, and its model is asked about the spring and winter stations. The example checks which of those stations the survey covered, and then how far off a random forest fitted to the survey is at each of them. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() surveyed <- filter(survey, season %in% c("summer", "autumn")) asked <- filter(survey, season %in% c("spring", "winter")) inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu") tibble(surveyed = nrow(surveyed), asked = nrow(asked)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| surveyed| asked| |--------:|-----:| | 394| 406|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from scipy.spatial.distance import cdist from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean, load_coastal_survey_truth survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() surveyed = survey[survey["season"].isin(["summer", "autumn"])].reset_index(drop=True) asked = survey[survey["season"].isin(["spring", "winter"])].reset_index(drop=True) inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] pd.DataFrame({"surveyed": [len(surveyed)], "asked": [len(asked)]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | surveyed | asked | |-----------:|--------:| | 394 | 406 | ::: ::: ::: ### Shallow, cold stations pass a range check but lie far from the survey A station deeper than any the survey reached is easy to spot: its depth is out of range. A new combination is harder. The distance uses the four measured inputs, standardised as in [Scaling and encoding](../02-marine-data/scaling-and-encoding.qmd) with chlorophyll logged first. A station is flagged as far from the survey when it lies further from it than 95% of surveyed stations lie from their nearest neighbour at another site (at another site, because a site's own visits sit close together). ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} distance_recipe <- recipe(surveyed[inputs]) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric()) |> step_log(chlorophyll_mg_m3) |> step_normalize(all_numeric()) |> prep() surveyed_scaled <- as.matrix(bake(distance_recipe, new_data = NULL)) asked_scaled <- as.matrix(bake(distance_recipe, asked)) # distance from each row of `from` to the nearest row of `to` nearest <- \(from, to) { apply(from, 1, \(row) min(sqrt(colSums((t(to) - row)^2)))) } # how far each surveyed station lies from the nearest at another site neighbour_gap <- map_dbl(seq_len(nrow(surveyed)), \(i) { other_sites <- surveyed$site_id != surveyed$site_id[i] nearest(surveyed_scaled[i, , drop = FALSE], surveyed_scaled[other_sites, ]) }) limit <- quantile(neighbour_gap, 0.95) in_range <- \(column) { seen <- range(surveyed[[column]], na.rm = TRUE) is.na(asked[[column]]) | between(asked[[column]], seen[1], seen[2]) } asked <- asked |> mutate(distance = nearest(asked_scaled, surveyed_scaled), far = distance > limit, every_range = reduce(map(inputs, in_range), `&`)) asked |> summarise(stations = n(), `inside every range` = sum(every_range), `far from the survey` = sum(far), `inside every range but far` = sum(every_range & far)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| inside every range| far from the survey| inside every range but far| |--------:|------------------:|-------------------:|--------------------------:| | 406| 279| 243| 132|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def logged(frame): return frame[inputs].assign( chlorophyll_mg_m3=np.log(frame["chlorophyll_mg_m3"])) distance_recipe = Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler()), ]).fit(logged(surveyed)) surveyed_scaled = distance_recipe.transform(logged(surveyed)) asked_scaled = distance_recipe.transform(logged(asked)) # how far each surveyed station lies from the nearest at another site gaps = cdist(surveyed_scaled, surveyed_scaled) same_site = surveyed["site_id"].to_numpy()[:, None] == surveyed["site_id"].to_numpy() gaps[same_site] = np.inf limit = np.quantile(gaps.min(axis=1), 0.95) def in_range(column): low, high = surveyed[column].min(), surveyed[column].max() return asked[column].isna() | asked[column].between(low, high) asked["distance"] = cdist(asked_scaled, surveyed_scaled).min(axis=1) asked["far"] = asked["distance"] > limit asked["every_range"] = np.logical_and.reduce([in_range(c) for c in inputs]) pd.DataFrame({ "stations": [len(asked)], "inside every range": [asked["every_range"].sum()], "far from the survey": [asked["far"].sum()], "inside every range but far": [(asked["every_range"] & asked["far"]).sum()], }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | inside every range | far from the survey | inside every range but far | |-----------:|---------------------:|----------------------:|-----------------------------:| | 406 | 279 | 243 | 132 | ::: ::: ::: Of the 406 spring and winter stations, 279 pass the range check on every input. Yet 132 of those, 47% of the stations that pass, are far from every surveyed station, and 97 of those are winter stations. @fig-novelty shows why. In summer and autumn shallow water is warm, so the survey met cold water only at depth. Winter cools the shallow water to temperatures the survey recorded, at depths it covered, but never together. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} novelty <- asked |> mutate(status = case_when( !every_range ~ "Outside a range", far ~ "Inside every range, far from the survey", .default = "Close to surveyed stations" )) ggplot(mapping = aes(depth_m, temperature_c)) + annotate("rect", xmin = min(surveyed$depth_m, na.rm = TRUE), xmax = max(surveyed$depth_m, na.rm = TRUE), ymin = min(surveyed$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE), ymax = max(surveyed$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE), fill = NA, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linetype = "dashed") + geom_point(data = surveyed, colour = "grey75", size = 1.2) + geom_point(aes(colour = status), data = novelty, size = 1.6, alpha = 0.85) + scale_colour_manual(values = c( "Close to surveyed stations" = ml_palette[["sky"]], "Outside a range" = ml_palette[["blue"]], "Inside every range, far from the survey" = ml_palette[["orange"]] )) + guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) + labs(x = "Depth (m)", y = "Temperature (°C)", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Depth against temperature for the summer and autumn survey (grey) and the spring and winter stations its model is asked about. The dashed box is the survey's range of each input taken alone. Orange stations are inside every range yet far from any surveyed station; most are shallow and cold, a combination the survey did not meet, as its cold water was all deep.](sampling-and-extrapolation_files/figure-html/fig-novelty-1.png){#fig-novelty fig-alt='A scatter plot with depth from 0 to 200 metres on the horizontal axis and temperature from about 2 to 16 degrees on the vertical. Grey points, the summer and autumn survey, form a band that cools with depth, from about 10 to 16 degrees in shallow water to 6 to 11 degrees at 150 metres. A dashed box marks the survey\'s range of depth and temperature. Spring and winter stations are coloured: light blue ones, close to surveyed stations, sit along the lower edge of the grey band; dark blue ones, outside a range, lie mostly below the box, colder than any surveyed station, at depths beyond 90 metres; orange ones, inside every range but far from the survey, form a band beneath the grey points between the surface and about 100 metres, at 5 to 8 degrees, where the survey has no stations.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: ### The random forest's error grows with distance from the survey A random forest fitted to the summer and autumn survey predicts the spring and winter stations. Season itself is left out of its inputs, as the survey has none of the seasons asked about. The survey is simulated, so its predictions can be compared with the **true mean count** at each station: the number the simulation drew that station's count around. No real study has this; it shows the forest's error free of the noise in single counts. The stations are compared in four groups, from the nearest quarter to the furthest. The error is the factor a prediction is off by: one twice the truth and one half of it are both off by a factor of 2. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} season_forest <- workflow( recipe(abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate, data = surveyed) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()), rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("regression") ) |> fit(surveyed) by_distance <- asked |> mutate(predicted = predict(season_forest, asked)$.pred) |> left_join(load_coastal_survey_truth(), by = "station_id") |> mutate(quarter = ntile(distance, 4), off_by = exp(abs(log(predicted / true_mean)))) |> summarise(stations = n(), `distance from` = min(distance), to = max(distance), `typical factor off` = median(off_by), .by = quarter) |> arrange(quarter) by_distance |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| quarter| stations| distance from| to| typical factor off| |-------:|--------:|-------------:|----:|------------------:| | 1| 102| 0.12| 0.62| 1.38| | 2| 102| 0.63| 0.99| 1.77| | 3| 101| 1.00| 1.35| 2.18| | 4| 101| 1.35| 3.29| 2.87|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} season_inputs = inputs + ["substrate"] season_forest = Pipeline([ ("recipe", ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), inputs), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["substrate"]), ])), ("model", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, random_state=1, n_jobs=-1)), ]).fit(surveyed[season_inputs], surveyed["abundance"]) by_distance = asked.assign( predicted=season_forest.predict(asked[season_inputs]) ).merge(load_coastal_survey_truth(), on="station_id") by_distance["quarter"] = pd.qcut(by_distance["distance"], 4, labels=[1, 2, 3, 4]) by_distance["off_by"] = np.exp(np.abs(np.log(by_distance["predicted"] / by_distance["true_mean"]))) (by_distance.groupby("quarter", observed=True) .agg(stations=("distance", "size"), distance_from=("distance", "min"), to=("distance", "max"), typical_factor_off=("off_by", "median")) .round(2).reset_index()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | quarter | stations | distance_from | to | typical_factor_off | |----------:|-----------:|----------------:|-----:|---------------------:| | 1 | 102 | 0.12 | 0.62 | 1.39 | | 2 | 101 | 0.63 | 0.99 | 1.87 | | 3 | 101 | 0.99 | 1.34 | 2.32 | | 4 | 102 | 1.35 | 3.3 | 3.15 | ::: ::: ::: At the quarter of stations nearest the survey, the forest is typically off by a factor of 1.4. At the furthest quarter it is typically off by 2.9. The forest reports nothing different at the far stations; the distance is the only sign that its predictions there deserve less trust. ## A prediction map should show where it extrapolates Mapped alongside a prediction, the distance to the nearest surveyed station shows where the map rests on the survey and where it is extrapolating; areas far from the survey can be greyed out or left unmapped. [Spatial and temporal cross-validation](../07-validation/spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd) holds out whole areas of the map, so that a score is measured on stations as far from the fitted data as the area to be mapped. When extrapolating is the point, as in projecting a species' range under warmer water than any survey recorded, say which predictions are extrapolations and expect errors larger than any cross-validation on the survey has measured. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Survey effort is uneven, and in **extrapolation** a model answers for conditions its survey never covered. Nothing in its predictions shows that it has left the data. - A range check on each input misses new combinations: of the 279 spring and winter stations that passed it, 132 were far from every surveyed station. The **distance to the nearest surveyed station**, on standardised inputs, flags them. - The forest's typical error grew from a factor of 1.4 at the nearest quarter of stations to 2.9 at the furthest. Map that distance with the predictions, and treat areas far from the survey as extrapolation. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Flag stations with a stricter limit, `quantile(neighbour_gap, 0.99)` (`0.99` in `np.quantile()` in Python). How many of the stations that pass the range check are still far from the survey? 2. Measure how far each station deeper than 100 m lies from a survey of the stations shallower than 100 m, with `nearest()` (`cdist()` in Python) and a `distance_recipe` built on the shallow stations. Do the deepest stations lie furthest from the survey?
